note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. You may use a calculator unless your instructor says otherwise. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A room attendant puts 4 bath towels in each of 12 villa bathrooms. How many towels are needed?
A hotel restaurant serves 86 breakfasts on Monday, 74 on Tuesday and 91 on Wednesday. How many breakfasts is that in total?
The store room has 240 bottles of water. 165 bottles are sent to the villas. How many bottles are left?
156 bread rolls are shared equally among 12 banquet tables. How many rolls does each table get?
Work out 5 + 3 × 4.
A cake recipe uses 3/4 of a bag of flour. The pastry cook makes half of the recipe. What fraction of the bag is used?
A chef needs 1/4 kg of butter. What is 1/4 written as a decimal?
A 1.5 kg block of cheese is cut into three equal pieces. How heavy is each piece?
A rum cake is cut into 12 equal slices, and the guests eat 8 slices. What fraction of the cake is left?
A pastry cook weighs 1.25 kg of flour and 0.75 kg of sugar. What is the total weight?
One bottle of juice costs J$185.50. What do 4 bottles cost?
A bag of flour weighs 3.47 kg. Round this to one decimal place.
How many grams are there in 2.5 kg of rice?
A jug holds 1.5 litres of sorrel. How many 250 ml glasses can be filled from it?
A bottle of syrup holds 750 ml. How many litres is this?
An old recipe says to bake a cake at 350 °F. About what is this in degrees Celsius?
What is 10% of J$8 500?
A guest's restaurant bill is J$12 000. A 10% service charge is added. What is the total?
A villa costs US$400 a night. For a long stay, the owner gives 25% off. What is the new nightly rate?
A trainee scores 52 out of 80 on a test. What percentage is this?
A hotel has 50 rooms, and 40 of them are occupied tonight. What is the occupancy percentage?
The ingredients for a plate of jerk chicken cost J$600. The dish sells for J$2 000. What percentage of the selling price is the food cost?
A floor cleaner is mixed 1 part concentrate to 9 parts water. How much concentrate is in 1 litre of the mixed solution?
A fruit punch uses 2 parts juice to 1 part soda water. How much soda water goes with 4 litres of juice?
A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of rice. How much rice is needed for 10 people?
5 kg of Irish potatoes cost J$1 250. At the same price, what do 8 kg cost?
Two room attendants take 6 hours to clean a large villa. How long would 3 room attendants take, working at the same rate?
A 2 kg whole chicken loses 30% of its weight in bones and trimming. How much usable meat is left?
A pot holds 4.5 kg of rice and peas. Each portion is 150 g. How many portions can be served?
A buffet table is 2.4 m long and 0.8 m wide. What length of table skirting goes right round its four sides (the perimeter)?
A villa bedroom floor is 5 m long and 4 m wide. What is its area?
One litre of floor polish covers 40 m². How many litres are needed for a hotel lobby floor of 120 m²?
A villa plunge pool is 3 m long, 2 m wide and 1 m deep. How many litres does it hold when full? (1 m³ = 1 000 litres)
A round cake is 20 cm across (its diameter). About how long must a ribbon be to go once round it? (π is about 3.14)
A guest buys 4 gift baskets at J$1 980 each in the hotel shop. Which is the best quick estimate of the total?
Round J$3 460 to the nearest hundred dollars.
A guest pays a J$3 650 bar bill with a J$5 000 note. How much change is due?
A guest wants to pay a US$ bill in Jamaican dollars. The front desk has the day's rate in J$ for each US$1. What must the cashier do?
options: Multiply the US$ amount by the day's rate
Divide the US$ amount by the day's rate
Add the day's rate to the US$ amount
Charge the same number, but in J$

questions.stem: A wedding reception starts at 19:30 and lasts 2 hours 45 minutes. When does it end?
A cook works from 06:00 to 14:30 with a 30-minute meal break. How many hours does the cook work?
A guest checks in on 12 March and checks out on 17 March. How many nights is the stay?
The breakfast numbers for four days are 120, 135, 110 and 155. What is the average (mean) per day?
The room service menu shows: club sandwich J$1 800, fresh juice J$650. A guest orders 2 sandwiches and 3 juices. What is the total?
Why should you check a bill or a recipe calculation, for example by estimating or working it backwards?
options: To catch mistakes before they cost money or upset a guest
Because a calculator is never right on the first try
So that every answer comes out as a whole number
To make the working look longer on the page

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences and show your working. You may use a calculator unless your instructor says otherwise. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is 20% of J$4 500? Give the answer in J$.
How many 50 ml portions of sauce can be filled from a 2 litre bottle?
A square lobby floor tile is 300 mm on each side. What is its area in square metres?
What is the name of a straight line from the centre of a circle to its edge, for example on a round cake board?
What is the value of π (pi), correct to two decimal places?
Write the ratio 12 : 18 in its simplest form.
A slow-cooked dish takes 3.5 hours. How many minutes is that?
A guest's flight leaves at 18:45. Write this time in 12-hour time.
accepted: quarter to seven in the evening

shortAnswers.stem: A triangular flower bed at a villa has a base of 6 m and a height of 4 m. What is its area in square metres?
A 7.5 kg sack of rice is packed into 0.5 kg bags. How many bags can be filled?
A standard recipe makes 24 festivals. How many batches are needed to make 120 festivals?
A guest stays 4 nights at US$250 a night. What is the room charge in US$, before any taxes?

essays.stem: Explain how to work out how much of a food to order for a function, including extra for waste. Use a worked example from a hotel or villa kitchen.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the number of guests and the portion size for each dish in the standard recipe. Then I would multiply the portion size by the number of guests to find the total amount. Next I would add extra for waste, spills and second helpings, often about 10%, or as the kitchen's policy says. Last I would round up to the pack sizes that the supplier sells. For example, a villa wedding has 60 guests and each portion of rice is 150 g. 60 × 150 g = 9 000 g, which is 9 kg. Adding 10%: 9 kg × 0.10 = 0.9 kg, so 9 + 0.9 = 9.9 kg. Rice comes in 2 kg bags, and 9.9 ÷ 2 = 4.95, so I would order 5 bags (10 kg). Before ordering, I would check the store room, so that I order only what is not already in stock.
markingPoints: Finds the number of guests and the portion size
Multiplies the portion size by the number of guests to find the total
Adds an allowance for waste (for example 10%)
Rounds up to the pack sizes that can be bought
Correct worked example with the working shown

essays.stem: Describe the order of operations (often remembered as BODMAS). Show how to use it to work out 20 − 4 × (3 + 2), and give one example from a guest bill.
essays.modelAnswer: When a calculation has more than one operation, they must be done in the right order or the answer will be wrong. BODMAS gives the order: Brackets first, then Orders (powers and roots), then Division and Multiplication working from left to right, and last Addition and Subtraction working from left to right. For 20 − 4 × (3 + 2), I work out the brackets first: 3 + 2 = 5, so the sum becomes 20 − 4 × 5. Next I multiply: 4 × 5 = 20, so it becomes 20 − 20. Last I subtract: 20 − 20 = 0. The answer is 0. On a guest bill, 2 dinners at J$3 000 and 1 dessert at J$800 is 2 × 3 000 + 800. I multiply first, 2 × 3 000 = 6 000, then add 800, so the total is J$6 800. Adding first would give 2 × 3 800 = J$7 600, which overcharges the guest.
markingPoints: Explains why an order is needed and gives the BODMAS order correctly
Works out the brackets first (5)
Then multiplies (20), then subtracts
Correct final answer of 0
Correct guest bill example (multiplies before adding)

essays.stem: Explain how to change between grams and kilograms, and between millilitres and litres. Give an example of each change from a kitchen or bar.
essays.modelAnswer: There are 1 000 grams in 1 kilogram and 1 000 millilitres in 1 litre. To change from a bigger unit to a smaller unit, I multiply by 1 000. To change from a smaller unit to a bigger unit, I divide by 1 000. For example, a recipe needs 1.25 kg of flour, and 1.25 × 1 000 = 1 250 g, so I set the scale to 1 250 g. A bag of sugar holds 450 g, and 450 ÷ 1 000 = 0.45 kg. At the bar, a jug of 2.5 litres of fruit punch is 2.5 × 1 000 = 2 500 ml. A can of soda holds 330 ml, which is 330 ÷ 1 000 = 0.33 litres. Before I add amounts together, or scale a recipe, I put them all into the same unit. I always write the unit beside every answer, so that nobody mistakes 0.5 kg for 0.5 g.
markingPoints: States 1 000 g = 1 kg and 1 000 ml = 1 L
Multiply to go to a smaller unit; divide to go to a bigger unit
Correct example for grams and kilograms
Correct example for millilitres and litres
Says to use the same unit throughout and write the unit

essays.stem: Explain what a ratio is and how to use one to mix a cleaning solution or a drink for guests. Give a worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: A ratio compares the amounts of two or more things. A ratio of 1 : 4 means 1 part of the first thing to 4 parts of the second. To use a ratio, I add the parts to find the total number of parts. Then I divide the amount I need by the total parts to find the size of one part. Last, I multiply one part by each number in the ratio. For example, a room attendant needs 500 ml of a cleaning solution mixed 1 : 4, concentrate to water. The total is 1 + 4 = 5 parts. One part is 500 ÷ 5 = 100 ml. So she needs 1 × 100 = 100 ml of concentrate and 4 × 100 = 400 ml of water. Check: 100 + 400 = 500 ml. I would measure with a marked jug, not guess, and always use the ratio on the maker's label.
markingPoints: Explains that a ratio compares amounts in parts
Adds the parts to find the total
Finds one part by dividing
Multiplies to get each amount, with a correct worked example
Measures accurately and follows the maker's ratio

essays.stem: Explain how to work out a percentage of an amount, and how to add or take away a percentage. Give worked examples using a guest bill and a discount.
essays.modelAnswer: Per cent means "out of 100". To find a percentage of an amount, I divide the percentage by 100 and multiply by the amount. For example, 10% of J$8 000 is 10 ÷ 100 × 8 000 = J$800. To add a percentage, such as a service charge, I work out the percentage and add it on. A dinner bill of J$8 000 with a 10% service charge is J$8 000 + J$800 = J$8 800. Another way is to multiply by 1.10. Taxes such as GCT are added in the same way, using the current rate. To take a percentage away, such as a discount, I work out the percentage and subtract it. A villa night at US$250 with 20% off: 20% of 250 is US$50, so the price is US$250 − US$50 = US$200. Another way is to multiply by 0.80. I check by estimating: 10% of about J$8 000 is about J$800.
markingPoints: Explains per cent as out of 100
Method to find a percentage of an amount
Correct example of adding a percentage (service charge)
Correct example of taking a percentage away (discount)
Checks by estimating, or shows the multiplier method

essays.stem: A standard recipe for rum cake makes 8 portions. Explain how to scale it to make 20 portions using a conversion factor, and show the working for two ingredients.
essays.modelAnswer: A conversion factor tells me how many times bigger or smaller the new recipe is. I find it by dividing the new number of portions by the old number: 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5. Then I multiply the amount of every ingredient by 2.5. For example, if the recipe uses 250 g of flour, I need 250 × 2.5 = 625 g. If it uses 4 eggs, I need 4 × 2.5 = 10 eggs. If it uses 200 g of butter, I need 200 × 2.5 = 500 g. I write the new amounts down as a new recipe card, so that nobody has to work them out again. I check that I have the right size and number of baking tins, because the baking time may change if the tins are bigger. Strong flavours such as spices may need care, so I taste and adjust where the recipe allows.
markingPoints: Conversion factor = new portions ÷ old portions
Correct factor of 2.5
Multiplies every ingredient by the factor
Correct working for at least two ingredients
Writes down the new recipe and checks tins, baking time or seasoning

essays.stem: Explain how to estimate an answer before using a calculator, and why estimating is useful at the front desk or in the kitchen.
essays.modelAnswer: To estimate, I round each number to an easy number, usually to the nearest 10, 100 or 1 000, and then do the sum in my head. For example, a function for 48 guests costs J$2 100 a head. I round 48 to 50 and J$2 100 to J$2 000, and 50 × 2 000 = J$100 000. The exact answer on the calculator is 48 × 2 100 = J$100 800, which is close to my estimate, so I can trust it. If the calculator had shown J$1 008 000 or J$10 080, I would know I had pressed a wrong key or put a zero in the wrong place. Estimating is useful because it catches big mistakes before a guest is overcharged or undercharged, or before too much food is ordered. It also helps when a guest asks for a rough price on the spot, and when checking that change given is about right.
markingPoints: Rounds numbers to easy values
Does the simpler sum in the head
Correct worked example
Compares with the exact answer to catch mistakes
Gives a reason or use for estimating at work

essays.stem: A room attendant must clean three villas, taking 1 hour 45 minutes, 2 hours 30 minutes and 50 minutes. She starts at 08:00 and takes a 30-minute break after the second villa. Work out when she finishes, and explain each step.
essays.modelAnswer: I add each time to the clock in turn. She starts at 08:00. The first villa takes 1 hour 45 minutes: 08:00 plus 1 hour is 09:00, plus 45 minutes is 09:45. The second villa takes 2 hours 30 minutes: 09:45 plus 2 hours is 11:45, plus 30 minutes is 12:15. Then she takes a 30-minute break: 12:15 plus 30 minutes is 12:45. The third villa takes 50 minutes: 12:45 plus 15 minutes is 13:00, and the other 35 minutes takes it to 13:35. So she finishes at 13:35, which is 1:35 p.m. Check: the total time is 1 h 45 min + 2 h 30 min + 30 min + 50 min = 5 hours 35 minutes, and 08:00 plus 5 hours 35 minutes is 13:35. I must remember that there are 60 minutes in an hour, not 100.
markingPoints: First villa done at 09:45
Second villa done at 12:15
Break ends at 12:45
Finishes at 13:35 (1:35 p.m.)
Checks the total, or explains 60 minutes to an hour

essays.stem: Explain how to work out the cost of one portion of a dish and its food cost percentage. Use a worked example with made-up prices.
essays.modelAnswer: First I list every ingredient in the standard recipe and the amount used. Then I work out the cost of each amount from the purchase prices, for example the price per kilogram times the kilograms used. I add these costs to get the total cost of the recipe. Next I divide the total by the number of portions to find the cost of one portion. Last, I find the food cost percentage: cost of one portion ÷ selling price × 100. For example, ackee and saltfish for 4 portions uses ackee costing J$1 200, saltfish costing J$1 000, and onion, sweet pepper, tomato and oil costing J$400. The total is J$2 600, and J$2 600 ÷ 4 = J$650 per portion. If the dish sells for J$2 200, the food cost is 650 ÷ 2 200 × 100 = about 30%. The kitchen compares this with its target to see if the price is right.
markingPoints: Lists every ingredient and works out the cost of the amount used
Adds the costs to get the recipe total
Divides by the number of portions
Food cost % = portion cost ÷ selling price × 100
Correct worked example

essays.stem: Describe ways to check that a calculation is correct, and explain why accuracy matters in hospitality work.
essays.modelAnswer: One way to check is to estimate first, by rounding the numbers, and see if the answer is close. Another way is to work backwards with the opposite operation. For example, if I work out the change from J$5 000 for a J$3 650 bill as J$1 350, I can check that J$3 650 + J$1 350 = J$5 000. I can also do the sum a second time, or ask a co-worker to check it. I check that all amounts are in the same unit and currency, and that the decimal point is in the right place. When scaling a recipe or mixing a chemical, I check the amounts again before I weigh or pour. Accuracy matters because a wrong bill upsets guests and loses money or trust, wrong change is a loss to the till, a wrong recipe wastes food, and a wrong chemical mix can damage surfaces or harm people.
markingPoints: Estimate and compare
Work backwards with the opposite operation
Repeat the sum, ask someone to check, or check units, currency and decimal point
Checks amounts again before weighing, mixing or charging
Gives reasons accuracy matters (guests, money, waste, safety)

practical1.title: Measure a guest room and work out the floor area, cleaning solution and cost
practical1.brief: As a group, measure the Centre's training guest room, or another room the assessor chooses, and work out how much floor cleaner is needed to clean it every day for a week, and what that costs. Each member measures at least one length with a tape measure while another member reads the tape to check it. Write every measurement in millimetres, then change it into metres. Draw a simple labelled sketch of the floor. Work out the floor area, and take away any part that is not cleaned, such as a fixed wardrobe. Use the figures on the assessor's card (for example, how much mixed solution is needed for each square metre, the mixing ratio on the label, and the price of the concentrate) to work out the amounts of concentrate and water for one clean, then for 7 days, and the cost for the week. Every member does at least one of the calculations, and another member checks it. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the working sheet once for the whole group.
materials: Tape measures (at least 2), 5 m or longer
Assessor's card with the solution needed per square metre, the mixing ratio and the price
Working sheet, pencils and an eraser
A sketch pad for a labelled sketch of the floor
photos: Each member measuring, with the tape against the wall or floor (one photo per member)
The labelled sketch with all measurements in millimetres
The working sheet showing the change to metres and the floor area
The working for the concentrate and water, using the ratio
The cost for the week worked out and checked, with initials of the checker
checklist: Measured accurately, holding the tape straight and reading it correctly
Wrote measurements clearly with the unit
Worked out the floor area correctly, showing the working
Used the ratio correctly to find the concentrate and water
Worked out the weekly cost correctly
Checked another member's calculation and corrected any mistake
Explained their own calculation to the assessor
safety: Do not let a steel tape snap back; its edge can cut
Do not stand on beds, chairs or tables to measure; use a step ladder only if the assessor allows and someone holds it
Move furniture only with help, bending the knees and keeping the back straight
Keep clear of any wet floor and its warning sign

practical2.title: Scale a fruit punch recipe, measure it out, and cost each glass and a guest bill
practical2.brief: As a group, scale and make a non-alcoholic fruit punch in the Centre's kitchen or bar, then cost it. The assessor gives a standard recipe for 10 glasses and asks for 25 glasses. First, on paper, work out the conversion factor and the new amount of each ingredient. Then wash your hands, measure each ingredient with marked jugs and scales, reading the jug at eye level, and mix the punch in a clean container. Each member measures at least one ingredient while another member checks the reading. Pour the punch into labelled, covered jugs and chill it at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says. Next, use the prices on the assessor's card to work out the cost of the batch and the cost of one 250 ml glass. Last, write a bill for a table of 6 guests who each have one glass, at the selling price on the card, with a 10% service charge, and show the total in J$ and in US$ using the practice exchange rate on the card. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the working sheet once for the whole group.
materials: Assessor's card with the standard recipe, prices, selling price and a practice exchange rate
Juices, syrup, water and fruit for the punch, as the recipe lists
Marked measuring jugs, a kitchen scale, a large clean container and jugs with lids
Labels and a marker; chopping board and knife if fruit is cut
Working sheet, bill pad and calculators
Cleaning cloths, sanitiser and a tray for spills
photos: The working on paper: conversion factor and new amounts
Each member measuring an ingredient, reading the jug or scale (one photo per member)
The finished punch in labelled, covered jugs in the fridge
The cost working for the batch and for one glass
The guest bill in J$ and US$, checked
The work area cleaned and the equipment put away
checklist: Worked out the conversion factor and the new amounts correctly
Measured accurately, reading jugs at eye level and using the scale correctly
Worked hygienically: washed hands, used clean equipment, covered and chilled the punch
Labelled the punch with its name and the date
Worked out the batch cost and the cost per glass correctly
Wrote the guest bill correctly, with the service charge and both currencies
Checked another member's working or measuring
safety: Wash your hands, tie back or cover your hair, and wear a clean apron
If fruit is cut, use a sharp knife on a steady board; carry knives point down and never try to catch a falling knife
Wipe up any spill at once so that nobody slips
Keep liquids away from calculators, phones and electrical sockets
